About the Journal

Focus and Scope

The journal publishes original research articles on teaching, learning, assessment and education policy in primary, secondary and higher education. Its readership is researchers, teacher educators and policy makers.

Open Access Policy

This journal provides immediate open access to its content on the principle that making research freely available to the public supports a greater global exchange of knowledge. All content is free to read, download and re-use for any lawful purpose, without registration and without embargo.

Peer Review Process

All research articles undergo double-anonymous peer review. Each manuscript is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers who are external experts in the field. The editor makes the final decision based on the reviewers' reports. Editorials are not subject to peer review. Authors may suggest potential reviewers.

Plagiarism Screening

All submissions are screened for plagiarism with Crossref Similarity Check (iThenticate) before review.

Publication Frequency

The journal is published twice a year, in June and December.

Copyright and Licensing

Authors retain copyright of their work without restrictions. Articles are published under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0), which allows anyone to share and adapt the work for any purpose with attribution.

Author Fees

The journal does not charge any fees: there are no article processing charges and no submission charges. Editorial decisions are independent of any payment.

Archiving

The journal content is preserved in the PKP Preservation Network (PKP PN) and in Portico for long-term digital preservation.

Repository Policy

Authors may deposit the submitted version, the accepted manuscript and the version of record in an institutional repository or a subject repository without embargo.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

Authors must disclose any use of generative AI tools in preparing a manuscript; AI tools cannot be listed as authors. Reviewers and editors must not upload manuscripts to generative AI tools.

Publication Ethics

The journal follows the COPE guidelines on authorship, complaints and appeals, misconduct, conflicts of interest, data sharing and reproducibility, ethical oversight including informed consent, intellectual property, post-publication discussion and corrections and retractions.

Advertising

The journal does not accept advertising.

Ownership and Management

The journal is owned by the Open Education Research Society and managed by its editorial office. It is funded by membership dues of the Society.

Publisher

Publisher: Open Education Research Society, 12 Harbour Street, Leeds LS1 4AB, United Kingdom.

Submissions

Author Guidelines

Manuscripts must be written in English. The journal considers original research articles and review articles. Authors should prepare the manuscript with the journal template and follow APA style. Authorship should follow the ICMJE criteria and every author's contribution is described with CRediT.

Submission Preparation Checklist

  • The submission has not been previously published.
  • The manuscript is anonymised for double-anonymous review.

Copyright Notice

Authors retain copyright and grant the journal the right of first publication under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

Author Fees

There are no article processing charges and no submission charges.

Bilingual instruction outcomes

  • Laura MorenoUniversity

DOI:

https://doi.org/10.5555/joer.1

Abstract

This study examines bilingual instruction outcomes. The study draws on a survey of 107 teachers and on interviews with school leaders in three regions. It describes how bilingual instruction outcomes is organised in practice, which conditions support it and which obstacles teachers report. The analysis combines descriptive statistics with a thematic analysis of the interviews. The results show that the approach is used more often in schools that provide time for collaboration, and that teachers who receive feedback from colleagues are more confident in their practice. The paper discusses the implications of these findings for teacher education, for school leadership and for education policy, and it identifies questions for further research.
